source_text:
»ἐν δὲ τῷ ἐρχομένῳ ζωή[ν] ἐστιν αἰώνιος.«
»Εσονται οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι.« τοῦτο πολύχουν μέν ἐστι κατὰ τὴν ὑπόνοιαν καὶ τὸν σαφηνισμόν, οὐ μὴν ἔν γε τῷ παρόντι τὴν ζήτησιν ἀπαιτεῖ· οὐ γὰρ μόνον ῥέπει πρὸς τοὺς πολυκτήμονας, ἀλλ᾿ ἁπλῶς πρὸς ἅπαντας ἀνθρώπους τοὺς πίστει καθάπαξ ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιδιδόντας. ὥστε τοῦτο μὲν ἀνακείσθω τὰ νῦν. τὸ δέ γε προκείμενον ἡμῖν οἶμαι μηδέν τι ἐνδεέστερον τῆς ἐπαγγελίας δεδεῖχθαι, ὅτι τοὺς πλουσίους οὐδένα τρόπον ὁ σωτὴρ κατ᾿ αὐτόν γε τὸν πλοῦτον καὶ τὴν περιβολὴν τῆς κτήσεως ἀποκέκλεικεν οὐδ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἀποτετάφρευκεν τὴν σωτηρίαν, εἴ γε δύναιντο καὶ βούλοιντο ὑποκύπτειν τοῦ θεοῦ ταῖς ἐντολαῖς καὶ τῶν προσκαίρων προτιμῷεν τὴν ἑαυτῶν ζωὴν καὶ βλέποιεν πρὸς τὸν κύριον ἀτενεῖ τῷ βλέμματι, καθάπερ εἰς ἀγαθοῦ κυβερνήτου νεῦμα δεδορκότες, τί βούλεται, τί προστάσσει, τί σημαίνει, τί δίδωσι τοῖς αὑτοῦ ναύταις [τὸ] σύνθημα, ποῦ καὶ πόθεν τὸν ὅρμον ἐπαγγέλλεται. τί γὰρ ἀδικεῖ τις, εἰ προσέχων τὴν γνώμην καὶ φειδόμενος πρὸ τῆς πίστεως βίον ἱκανὸν συνελέξατο; ἢ καὶ τὸ τούτου μᾶλλον ἀνέγκλητον, εἰ εὐθὺς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ τὴν τύχην νέμοντος εἰς οἶκον τοιούτων ἀνθρώπων εἰσῳκίσθη καὶ γένος ἀμφιλαφὲς τοῖς χρήμασιν [ἰσχῦον] καὶ τῷ πλούτῳ κρατοῦν; εἰ γὰρ διὰ τὴν ἀκούσιον ἐν πλούτῳ γένεσιν ἀπελήλαται ζωῆς, ἀδικεῖται μᾶλλον ὑπὸ τοῦ γειναμένου θεοῦ, προσκαίρου μὲν ἡδυπαθείας κατηξιωμένος, ἀιδίου δὲ ζωῆς ἀπεστερημένος, τί δ᾿ ὅλως πλοῦτον ἐχρῆν ἐκ γῆς ἀνατεῖλαί ποτε, εἰ χορηγὸς καὶ πρόξενός ἐστι θανάτου; ἀλλ᾿ εἰ δύναταί τις ἐνδοτέρω τῶν ὑπαρχόντων κάμπτειν τῆς ἐξουσίας καὶ μέτρια φρονεῖν καὶ σωφρονεῖν καὶ θεὸν μόνον ζητεῖν καὶ θεὸν ἀναπνεῖν καὶ θεῷ συμπολιτεύεσθαι. πτωχὸς οὗτος παρέστηκε ταῖς ἐντολαῖς, ἐλεύθερος, ἀήττητος, ἄνοσος, ἄτρωτος ὑπὸ χρημάτων· εἰ δὲ μή, θᾶττον κάμηλος διὰ βελόνης εἰσελεύσεται ἢ ὁ τοιοῦτος πλούσιος ἐπὶ τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ παρελεύσεται.
thought_title: Wealth itself does not bar the rich from salvation
orientation: Clement is concluding his argument that the Savior has not shut out the rich because of their wealth, and is now explaining that no one is wronged by being born rich, since what matters is the soul's disposition toward God.
pass_a_gloss: "But in the coming age there is eternal life." "The first shall be last and the last first." This saying is rich in meaning according to its hidden sense and its clarification, but it does not demand inquiry at the present moment; for it applies not only to those who possess much, but simply to all human beings who once for all give themselves over to faith. So let this matter be set aside for now. But the matter before us, I think, has been shown to be in no way inferior to the promise, that the Savior has in no manner shut out the rich because of wealth itself and the abundance of possession, nor has he cut off salvation from them by a trench, if indeed they are able and willing to bow under the commandments of God and to prefer their own life to temporary things and to look toward the Lord with a fixed gaze, as those who have fixed their eyes on the signal of a good helmsman, what he wishes, what he commands, what he signifies, what signal he gives to his own sailors, where and from what point he promises the anchorage. For what wrong does someone do, if by paying attention to his judgment and being sparing before faith he collected a sufficient livelihood? Or is it even more blameless than this, if immediately by God who allots fortune he was settled into the house of such people and a family abounding in money and prevailing in wealth? For if because of involuntary birth in wealth he has been driven away from life, he is wronged rather by the God who begot him, having been deemed worthy of temporary pleasure but deprived of eternal life. And why at all should wealth ever have sprung up from the earth, if it is the supplier and agent of death? But if someone is able to bend the power of his possessions inward and to think moderate things and to be self-controlled and to seek God alone and to breathe God and to live as a citizen with God, this poor person stands by the commandments, free, unconquered, without sickness, unwounded by money; but if not, sooner will a camel enter through a needle's eye than such a rich person will pass into the kingdom of God.

lemmas.gloss: rich in meaning, abundant in sense
has cut off by a trench, has fenced off
to bow under, to submit to
to live as a citizen with, to share civic life with

choices.english: has cut off salvation from them by a trench
choices.why: The verb ἀποταφρεύω means to fence off or cut off by a trench; rendering it literally preserves the military metaphor of a defensive ditch that Clement uses to say salvation has not been walled off from the rich.
rejected: has dug a moat around salvation

choices.english: to bow under the commandments of God
choices.why: The verb ὑποκύπτω means to stoop or bow under, conveying willing submission; the literal rendering keeps the physical image of bending beneath the yoke of the commandments.
rejected: to submit to the commandments of God
to obey the commandments of God

choices.why: ἀτενής means strained, fixed, intent; the phrase describes looking at the Lord with unwavering attention, matching the nautical image of sailors watching the helmsman's signal.
σύνθημα is an agreed sign or signal, especially in military or nautical contexts; rendering it as 'signal' fits the helmsman image Clement develops.
ἀμφιλαφής means ample, extensive, abounding; the literal rendering preserves the sense of a family richly supplied with material goods.
The phrase is striking and unusual; rendering it literally preserves Clement's vivid image of a soul so oriented to God that its very breath is God.

bible_refs.note: Ἔσονται οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι
θᾶττον κάμηλος διὰ βελόνης εἰσελεύσεται ἢ ὁ τοιοῦτος πλούσιος ἐπὶ τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ παρελεύσεται

pass_b_english: "But in the age that is coming there is eternal life."

"The first will be last and the last first" (Mark 10:31). This saying is rich in meaning, both in its hidden sense and in its clear explanation, but it does not need to be examined right now. It applies not only to those who possess much, but simply to all human beings who give themselves over to faith once for all. So let us set this matter aside for the present.

What we have set before us, I think, has been shown to be in no way inferior to the promise. The Savior has in no way shut out the rich because of wealth itself or the surrounding of possessions, nor has he cut off salvation from them by a trench—if they are able and willing to bow under the commandments of God, to prefer their own life to temporary things, and to look toward the Lord with a fixed gaze, like sailors watching the signal of a good helmsman to see what he wants, what he commands, what he signals, what sign he gives to his own sailors, and where and from what direction he promises the harbor.

For what wrong does someone do if, by paying attention to his judgment and being sparing before faith, he collected a sufficient livelihood? Or is his case even more blameless if God, who allots fortune, settled him immediately into the house of such people, into a family abounding in money and prevailing in wealth? If someone is driven away from life because of an involuntary birth into wealth, then he is wronged by the very God who begot him—deemed worthy of temporary pleasure but deprived of eternal life. And why should wealth ever have sprung up from the earth at all, if it is the supplier and agent of death?

But if someone is able to bend the power of his possessions inward, to think moderate thoughts, to be self-controlled, to seek God alone, to breathe God, and to live as a citizen with God, then this man stands before the commandments as a poor person—free, unconquered, without sickness, unwounded by money. But if not, a camel will enter through a needle's eye more quickly than such a rich person will pass into the kingdom of God (Mark 10:25).

problems.quote: to prefer their own life to temporary things
problems.source_quote: προτιμῆναι τὰ προσκαίρα τὴν ἑαυτῶν ζωήν
problems.why: Greek means preferring perishable things to one's life, opposite of English.
problems.fix: to prefer the perishable things to one's own life
problems.ruling: προτιμῇν τὰ προσκαίρα τὴν ἑαυτῶν ζωήν = prefer temporal things to one's life; English reverses the comparison, changing meaning.

edits.old: to prefer their own life to temporary things
edits.new: to prefer temporary things to their own life

fixed: Corrected the mistranslation: the Greek means preferring temporary things to one's own life, not the reverse.

problems.quote: to prefer temporary things to their own life
problems.why: The Greek says they should "prefer their own life," not "temporary things"; the added phrase changes the meaning.
problems.fix: change to "to prefer their own life".

problems.quote: "The first will be last and the last first" (Matthew 19:30).
problems.source_quote: Εσονται οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι.
problems.why: Clement's source is Mark 10:31; citing Matthew 19:30 is a possible parallel but not the primary source.
problems.fix: "The first will be last and the last first" (Mark 10:31).
problems.ruling: English cites Matthew 19:30, but Clement’s Greek aligns with Mark 10:31; mis‑referencing scripture misleads readers.

problems.quote: a camel will enter through a needle's eye more quickly than such a rich person will pass into the kingdom of God (Matthew 19:24).
problems.source_quote: θᾶττον κάμηλος διὰ βελόνης εἰσελεύσεται ἢ ὁ τοιοῦτος πλούσιος ἐπὶ τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ παρελεύσεται
problems.why: Clement's source is Mark 10:25, not Matthew 19:24; he quotes Mark throughout.
problems.ruling: English cites Matthew 19:24, yet Clement’s source matches Mark 10:25; incorrect citation of verse is a factual error.

edits.old: to prefer temporary things to their own life
edits.new: to prefer their own life to temporary things

fixed: The Greek προτιμῷεν τὴν ἑαυτῶν ζωὴν means 'prefer their own life,' and the following genitive τῶν προσκαίρων means 'to temporary things,' so the English should read 'to prefer their own life to temporary things.'
Clement's source for 'The first will be last and the last first' is Mark 10:31, not Matthew 19:30.
Clement's source for the camel saying is Mark 10:25, not Matthew 19:24.

last_rejected.quote: then he is wronged by the very God who begot him
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀδικεῖται μᾶλλον ὑπὸ τοῦ γειναμένου θεοῦ
last_rejected.why: Source says 'rather he is wronged' (μᾶλλον); English drops 'rather,' losing Clement's argument that this conclusion follows.
last_rejected.fix: then he is rather wronged by the very God who begot him
last_rejected.ruling: Greek adds μᾶλλον “more/rather,” but English still conveys the main claim; omission is a nuance, not a change of meaning

last_rejected.quote: nor has he cut off salvation from them by a trench
last_rejected.why: The Greek says he has not cut off salvation; no reference to a trench is present.
last_rejected.fix: nor has he cut off salvation from them
last_rejected.ruling: ἀποτετάφρευκεν derives from ἀποταφρεύω, literally 'to cut off by a trench/ditch'; 'trench' is the word's proper meaning, not an addition.
